name: Quotation & Attribution Usage
description: Analyzes the frequency, context, and structural application of quotation marks. Large Language Models frequently abuse quotation marks in highly specific ways: they use 'scare quotes' to distance themselves from colloquialisms or idioms, they enclose overly common phrases in quotes to simulate academic rigor, and they often invent (hallucinate) perfectly formatted but non-existent quotes to support arguments.
mechanism: The algorithm extracts all text enclosed in single or double quotation marks and evaluates the surrounding context. It calculates the 'Scare Quote Ratio' (quotes around single, non-technical colloquial words) and the 'Attribution Density' (frequency of quotes tied to named entities). AI models, constrained by safety and neutrality alignments, are extremely hesitant to use informal language natively; if forced, they will almost always wrap slang or idioms in quotes to signal that the tone is borrowed, not inherent. Furthermore, when generating explanatory text, AI often over-quotes basic concepts to appear authoritative, whereas humans reserve quotes for direct speech or highly specific definitions.
useCase: Highly effective for auditing essays, opinion pieces, and literature reviews where AI's tendency to clinically isolate 'informal' words or hallucinate precise dialogue strings betrays its non-human origin.
strengths:
• Excellent at detecting the 'cautious AI' persona that refuses to use idioms naturally.
• Provides strong forensic evidence when combined with 'Named Entity Consistency', easily flagging hallucinated citations.
limitations:
• Susceptible to false positives in genuine journalistic writing, academic papers with heavy citations, or dialogue-heavy creative writing.
• Can be bypassed if the user explicitly instructs the AI to drop all quotation marks.
parameters:
Analysis: Orthographic Boundary Extraction and Contextual NLP Parsing
Metric: Frequency of Semantic Isolation ('Scare Quotes') and Density of Attribution
Output: 0-100 Quotation Predictability (Artificial Formatting) Score
accuracy: Moderate — 65-80% standalone accuracy. It is a powerful secondary indicator when analyzing formal essays or academic writing that feels suspiciously 'sterile'.

references.title: Bhattacharjee, A. et al. (2024). LLMs as Hallucination Generators: A Comprehensive Study. arXiv.
